result: Women live longer than men across human populations and nonhuman mammals, with lower biological ages as assessed by molecular biomarkers. This survival advantage is reflected in an increasing sex ratio with age (~50 men per 100 women among 90-year-olds, ~25 among 100-year-olds) and persists despite improved healthcare systems.
evaluation: Claims C3-C9 collectively establish the female survival advantage through demographic data (C8), cross-species evidence (C7), molecular biomarker assessments (C4), and persistence despite healthcare improvements (C9). The convergence of demographic, molecular, and comparative evidence provides strong support for this fundamental sex difference in aging.

result: Despite living longer, women are frailer and have worse health at the end of life compared to men, who perform better in physical function examinations. However, women tolerate frailty better, with men being more vulnerable to death at any given level of frailty—a phenomenon termed the 'sex-frailty paradox.'
evaluation: Claims C5-C6 and C187-C189 establish the sex-frailty paradox through multiple lines of evidence: women's higher frailty prevalence (C187), men's better physical performance (C6), and differential mortality vulnerability (C188). This paradox has been documented across multiple frailty scales and populations (C189), providing robust support for this counterintuitive finding.

result: Boys have shorter telomeres than girls at birth, a difference that persists throughout life. Telomeres are repeated DNA sequences at chromosome ends that shorten with cell division due to the end replication problem, eventually leading to cellular senescence. Short telomere length is associated with mortality, cardiovascular disease, and life stressors.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 establish the sex difference in telomere length with citation support, while C86-C90 provide the mechanistic basis for telomere biology. Claims C92-C94 demonstrate the health relevance of telomere length. The integration of sex differences, mechanism, and health outcomes provides comprehensive support for telomeres as a sex-dimorphic aging biomarker.

result: Boys/men have higher epigenetically predicted biological age than girls/women at all ages, consistent with the female survival advantage. This sex difference is apparent from childhood through adulthood and translates to differential mortality risk. In women, earlier menopause is associated with increased epigenetic age, while hormone replacement therapy is associated with lower epigenetic age.
evaluation: Claims C131-C133 establish the sex difference in epigenetic age across the lifespan with citation support (Horvath et al., 2016; Li et al., 2020b). Claims C134-C135 link this to hormonal factors through menopause and HRT effects (Levine et al., 2016). The consistency across ages and connection to mortality risk provides strong support for epigenetic age as a sex-dimorphic biomarker.

result: Women show higher mitochondrial gene expression, protein content, and overall activity in multiple tissues compared to men, with similar sexual dimorphism observed in rodent models. Estrogens influence mitochondrial function and exert protective effects, partly explaining delayed mitochondrial aging in women. Mitochondrial DNA abundance is elevated in premenopausal women and inversely associated with age, smoking, BMI, and frailty.
evaluation: Claims C82-C83 establish the sex difference in mitochondrial function across species with citation support (Ventura-Clapier et al., 2017). Claim C84 provides a mechanistic explanation through estrogen effects. Claim C85 adds population-level evidence from UK Biobank (Hägg et al., 2020) linking mitochondrial abundance to health outcomes. The convergence of human, animal, and mechanistic evidence strongly supports sex differences in mitochondrial aging.

result: Men experience more pronounced immunosenescence and inflammaging compared to women. Between puberty and menopause, women have lower infection rates, stronger immune responses, higher CD4+ T cell counts, and enhanced adaptive immune functions. However, women are more susceptible to autoimmune diseases. After menopause, autoimmune disease incidence in women decreases while chronic inflammatory disease incidence increases. Male immune cells show greater age-related decline, occurring 5-6 years earlier than in women.
evaluation: Claims C145-C154 establish comprehensive sex differences in immune aging through multiple lines of evidence: baseline immune parameters (C150-C151), infection susceptibility (C146), autoimmune disease patterns (C147-C148), and age-related changes (C152-C154). The temporal dynamics linked to hormonal changes and the genomic/epigenomic data (Márquez et al., 2020) provide strong mechanistic support for sex-dimorphic immune aging.

result: Men perform better in physical capability measures (grip strength, walking, stair climb) even after adjusting for body composition. Women have less skeletal muscle mass but men experience greater loss with aging. The Functional Aging Index (FAI), which combines multiple physical functions, is predictive of mortality in both sexes with a greater hazard ratio in women, though women have higher FAI scores indicating poorer functioning.
evaluation: Claims C169-C173 establish sex differences in physical function and muscle aging with citation support (Peiffer et al., 2010; Doherty, 2003). Claims C182-C183 provide an integrated measure (FAI) that captures the paradox: women have worse function but the rate of decline is similar (Finkel et al., 2019). This supports the broader sex-frailty paradox and demonstrates the complexity of sex differences in functional aging.

result: Sex steroids (androgens in men, estrogens and progestogens in women) exert lifelong influences beginning in utero, giving rise to sex differences in neuroanatomy and neurochemistry. Animal studies demonstrate that manipulating prenatal sex steroid levels causes permanent changes in neuronal architecture. Perinatal hormonal exposure plays a significant role in sex-specific metabolic programming, manifested as different risk profiles for metabolic diseases later in life.
evaluation: Claims C28-C34 establish the developmental origins of sex differences through hormonal mechanisms. The animal experimental evidence (C30, cited to Fitch and Denenberg, 1998) demonstrates causality, while C34 links prenatal exposure to adult disease risk (Dearden et al., 2018). The integration of developmental biology, experimental manipulation, and long-term health outcomes provides strong support for hormonal programming of sex differences.

result: Shorter reproductive lifespan in women is associated with decreased odds of longevity and higher cardiovascular disease risk, but lower risk of gynecological cancer mortality. Women with premature/early menopause have increased CVD risk before age 60 but not after 70. Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) shows age- and cause-varying effects: reduced mortality in younger women (<60 years) and for non-CVD/cancer causes, but diminishing benefits with increasing age.
evaluation: Claims C48-C54 establish complex, age-dependent relationships between reproductive lifespan, HRT, and health outcomes with citation support (Shadyab et al., 2017; Mishra et al., 2021; Wu et al., 2014; Zhu et al., 2019; Salpeter et al., 2004; Stram et al., 2011). The evidence demonstrates trade-offs between different health outcomes and the importance of timing, supporting the complexity of hormonal influences on aging.

result: Noncommunicable age-related diseases are now the leading causes of death worldwide in those over 70 years. Most cancers show sex-differentiated effects, with men having higher incidence and death rates for non-reproductive cancers. Premenopausal women are protected from cardiometabolic diseases, while Alzheimer's disease and other dementias are more prevalent in women, particularly in the oldest old.
evaluation: Claims C192-C193 establish the epidemiological landscape with WHO data. Claims C194, C196-C197, and C202 demonstrate sex-specific disease patterns with citation support (Aggarwal et al., 2018; Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2020; Mazure and Swendsen, 2016). The integration of epidemiological data with sex-specific patterns provides strong support for sex differences in age-related disease burden.

result: Longevity is moderately heritable. Rare germline mutational burden is associated with lifespan and healthspan, with the association between mutations and healthspan being more pronounced in women. Measured and genetically predicted levels of serum biomarkers are associated with healthspan and lifespan, again with stronger effects for healthspan in women.
evaluation: Claims C62-C65 establish genetic contributions to aging with sex-specific effects, supported by citations to recent studies (Melzer et al., 2020; Shindyapina et al., 2020; Li et al., 2021). The consistent finding of stronger healthspan associations in women across different genetic approaches (mutational burden and biomarker genetics) provides robust support for sex-dimorphic genetic influences on aging.

result: In mice, males have a higher number of senescent cells across life compared to females, though by the end of life, female senescent cell proportions approach male levels. Female stem cells show increased capacity for regeneration, self-renewal, and proliferation compared to males.
evaluation: Claims C108-C110 establish sex differences in cellular senescence and stem cell function with citation support (Yousefzadeh et al., 2020; Dulken and Brunet, 2015). However, the evidence is limited to animal models, and the manuscript notes the lack of human studies. The support is strong for animal models but extrapolation to humans requires caution.

result: Female mice show higher proteasome activity than males across nine tissues, with the largest sexual dimorphism in small intestine and kidney. Female fruit flies are more tolerant to oxidative stress with increased proteasome expression and activity, though this resistance is lost with age. Females in animal models exhibit more resistance to stressors, partly attributed to estrogen's beneficial effects.
evaluation: Claims C119-C122 establish sex differences in proteostasis across multiple species with citation support (Jenkins et al., 2020; Pomatto et al., 2017; Tower et al., 2020). The consistency across species and the mechanistic link to estrogen provide support. However, the manuscript notes the lack of human studies on proteostasis sexual dimorphism, limiting the generalizability.

result: Women have lower fasting insulin and glucose levels, lower basal fat oxidation, and different fat distribution (lower body) compared to men (visceral fat). Men's higher basal insulin levels promote greater muscle mass and strength. In rodents, males may have a more robust response to caloric restriction than females.
evaluation: Claims C160-C163 establish sex differences in metabolism and nutrient sensing with citation support (Comitato et al., 2015; Kane et al., 2018). The human metabolic differences are well-documented, though the caloric restriction response is based only on rodent studies. The mechanistic link between insulin, muscle mass, and sex differences is supported but the CR findings require human validation.

result: Women have historically been excluded from clinical trials due to safety concerns for pregnant/fertile women and hormonal fluctuations. This led to male-biased research, exemplified by cardiovascular disease research that produced risk calculations and guidelines not meeting women's needs. In animal research, male models are more common due to assumed female variability, but a large mouse study found sexual dimorphism in variability is trait-specific with neither sex being more variable overall.
evaluation: Claims C10-C14 establish the historical context of sex bias in research with citation support (Schenck-Gustafsson, 2009; Beery and Zucker, 2011; Zajitschek et al., 2020). The large mouse study (C14, 27,000 mice, 200+ traits) provides strong evidence against the assumed female variability justification. This supports the need for sex-inclusive research but is primarily methodological context rather than a biological finding.

result: A meta-analysis of sex differences in telomere length across 51 vertebrate species (mammals, birds, reptiles, fish) found no evidence supporting the heterogametic sex disadvantage or sexual selection hypotheses, and no associations supporting sex differences in longevity.
evaluation: Claims C101-C102 report findings from a large meta-analysis (Remot et al., 2020) that challenges theoretical explanations for sex differences in telomere length. While the meta-analysis is well-powered, this negative finding contrasts with the human data showing consistent sex differences in telomere length (C96-C97). The result is supported but highlights the complexity and species-specificity of telomere biology.

result: Women born during the Dutch Hunger Winter exhibit more unfavorable adiposity traits (higher BMI, waist circumference, disrupted lipid profiles) compared to men, while men show greater vulnerability to neurological damage. Girls' BMI is more affected by maternal overweight/obesity during pregnancy compared to boys.
evaluation: Claims C36-C38 establish sex-specific effects of prenatal nutrition on adult health outcomes, all supported by citation to Dearden et al., 2018. The Dutch Hunger Winter provides a natural experiment, though the findings are from a specific historical cohort. The sex-specific vulnerability patterns (metabolic in women, neurological in men) are intriguing but require replication in other contexts.

result: Over 4000 H3K9ac histone modification sites are associated with sex in human brain data. Genome-wide DNA methylation studies show significant sex differences in autosomes and X chromosome, linked to sexual dimorphism genes and X-inactivation. A meta-analysis found age-related sex differences in DNA methylation enriched in imprinted genes but not sex hormone-related genes, with sex-specific patterns in centenarians and Down syndrome samples. However, brain methylation studies found no sex-age interaction effects in Alzheimer's disease.
evaluation: Claims C136-C141 present mixed findings on epigenetic sex differences. The large number of sex-associated histone sites (C136) and genome-wide methylation differences (C137) are supported by citations (Klein et al., 2019; Li et al., 2020c; McCartney et al., 2019). However, the meta-analysis findings (C138-C140, Yusipov, 2020) show enrichment in imprinted but not hormone-related genes, which is somewhat unexpected. The negative finding for AD (C141, Pellegrini, 2020) adds complexity. The inconsistency across studies and tissues makes the overall picture uncertain.

result: Animal studies on sex differences in frailty show inconsistent results: some report higher frailty index scores in aged female mice, others report no difference, and one found higher scores in males.
evaluation: Claims C190-C191 report inconsistent findings from animal frailty studies, all cited to Heinze-Milne et al., 2019. The manuscript acknowledges the paucity of studies and variety in mouse strains as limitations. The inconsistency across studies prevents drawing firm conclusions about sex differences in frailty in animal models, contrasting with the consistent human findings (C187-C189).

result: The manuscript describes two main theories of aging: the senescent theory (including disposable soma, ROS theory, mutation accumulation, and rate of living) and the programmed theory (including Hayflick limit, central aging clock, and developmental processes). These theories provide frameworks for understanding aging mechanisms.
evaluation: Claims C15-C23 describe established aging theories with appropriate citations (Jin, 2010; Kirkwood and Shefferson, 2017; Liochev, 2013; Lints, 1989; Pearl, 2011; Bengtson and Settersten, 2016; Rattan, 2019; Feltes et al., 2015). These are well-established theoretical frameworks in gerontology. However, this is background knowledge rather than new findings, serving as context for interpreting sex differences in aging.

result: The review concludes that sex differences are consistently observed in biological aging research across species. Many aging markers are consistent with both programmed and senescent theories simultaneously. Both chromosomal and hormonal mechanisms explain sexual disparities. Cellular and molecular aging mechanisms are better maintained in women, though women catch up after menopause. Men show better functional aging related to muscle strength due to hormonal effects on muscle mass.
evaluation: Claims C210-C215 represent the authors' synthesis and conclusions from the review. These summary claims integrate evidence from throughout the manuscript (referenced to Table 1 and prior sections). While these are interpretive conclusions rather than primary findings, they are well-supported by the comprehensive evidence presented in the review. The conclusions appropriately acknowledge complexity and avoid oversimplification.

result: The National Institutes of Health now requires sex as a biological variable to be factored into research designs, analyses, and reporting. The Swedish Research Council has similar guidelines requiring applicants to describe whether sex and gender perspectives are relevant and how they will be included.
evaluation: Claims C216-C217 describe policy changes at major funding agencies with citation support (Pinn, 2020; The Swedish Research Council, 2020). These are factual statements about research policy rather than scientific findings. The claims are well-supported but represent administrative/policy context rather than biological discoveries.
